questions.q: Where does an `emit`-ted Solidity event actually get stored?
options: In the transaction's logs — a separate, cheaper-to-write section of the receipt, not contract state and not a return value
In a dedicated events table inside the contract's own storage
It isn't stored anywhere — events exist only during execution
It's sent directly to the caller's wallet as a push notification
questions.explain: Events are written into the logs bloom/receipt data, which is cheaper to write than contract storage and is never returned to the caller like a function return value.

questions.q: What does marking an event parameter `indexed` actually do?
options: Doubles the gas cost of every function call, with no other effect
Automatically triggers an email notification when the event fires
Lets logs be efficiently filtered by that parameter's value later (up to three per event)
Makes the parameter encrypted so only the emitting contract can read it
questions.explain: Indexed parameters go into the log's topics, which is what makes a query like "every Transfer to this address" cheap and filterable instead of a full scan.

questions.q: In ethers.js, what does `token.on("Transfer", callback)` do?
options: Runs the callback every time a matching Transfer event appears, with decoded arguments
Sends a new Transfer transaction on the contract's behalf
Immediately returns every past Transfer event as an array
Permanently subscribes the contract owner's wallet to transfer alerts
questions.explain: contract.on() registers a live listener that fires on future matching events; it does not fetch history (that's queryFilter).

questions.q: What's the relationship between a live event listener and a historical `queryFilter`/`getContractEvents` call?
options: A live listener automatically includes all historical events by default
Both are built on the same underlying eth_getLogs RPC data — one streams it live, the other fetches a snapshot
Historical queries only work on testnets, never mainnet
They use completely unrelated RPC methods with no shared data
questions.explain: Both ultimately query the same event log data; the difference is whether you're asking for new matches going forward or a one-time range in the past.

questions.q: A live listener started just now — will it see a Transfer event that happened yesterday?
options: Yes, all listeners automatically replay the last 30 days of events
It depends on the block's gas limit at the time
Yes, but only if the contract has fewer than 1000 total events
No — a live listener only sees events from the moment it starts; yesterday's event needs a historical query instead
questions.explain: A live `.on()`/`watchContractEvent` subscription only reacts to new matching logs going forward — past events require queryFilter or getContractEvents.
